utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] My apologies to all of you. It was an unexpected commitment that I had to deal with.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So any preliminaries before we bring the witness in? All right. So please, Madam Registrar, could you call the case, please?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, this is case number IT-99-36-T, the Prosecutor versus Radoslav Brdjanin.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Brdjanin, can you hear me in a language that you can understand? THE ACCUSED BRDJANIN: [Interpretation] Good morning. I hear and I understand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you and good morning to you. Appearances for the Prosecution?

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Good morning, Anna Richterova and Ann Sutherland for the Prosecution, assisted by Denise Gustin.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good morning to you. Appearances for accused Brdjanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. I'm John Ackerman along with my colleagues Milan Trbojevic and Marela Jevtovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Just for the record. I have not yet received any communication from Mr. Rohde regarding the matter raised by the Defence and that is why I have not mentioned it again. As soon as I am -- I receive the memo, then we will discuss the matter or we will act upon it, if necessary. So Mr. Usher, we ask you to bring the witness in, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good morning to you, Mr. Dedic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I apologise to you on behalf of the Tribunal for starting late or bringing you late in this courtroom. It was an urgent matter that I had to personally -- personal urgent matter that I had to it attend to and that is the reason. Before we continue with your testimony it, may I ask you to repeat the solemn declaration that you entered yesterday, please? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you. You may sit down. Ms. Sutherland will be proceeding with her examination-in-chief which shouldn't last long and then it will be followed by the cross-examination. Ms. Sutherland.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Examined by Ms. Sutherland: [Continued]:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Dedic, I want to go briefly back to an area I asked you questions about yesterday. You described your detention in the Nikola Mackic elementary school. When you entered the school, what if anything did you see on the walls?

utterances.speaker: SAMIR DEDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I saw that the walls were covered with blood and the floor as well. That was the first thing I noticed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I asked you yesterday whether you'd been questioned, and this is at LiveNote page 80 and you answered as to how they would take someone for questioning and that they wanted people to confess things. You then said many people had to confess because of the torture and mistreatment. Can you please tell Their Honours what happened to you during your questioning?

utterances.speaker: SAMIR DEDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can. These were their usual questions about weapons. They asked about things I didn't know about, how many rifles there were in the village, who fired at -- and so on. First of all, he asked me when I was born and then when I said it was in 1974, he said I was the youngest butcher from that village of mine, Crljeni and up until that time I didn't even kill a chicken, so it wasn't clear to me this question, it was frightening to me. I didn't know what to say. Then I was brought into a room. This is where the inspector was and they repeated the same questions. If I had a rifle, who had weapons, but this was accompanied by torture, by beatings. They would hit me on the legs, on my head. I received a very powerful blow to the back of my head and to this day I have problems with that. I have headaches. So this didn't last too long. And then I was returned to the hole again.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What were they hitting you with?

utterances.speaker: SAMIR DEDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Soldiers' boots, batons, with their fists. Whatever they would hit me with.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, moving on it to the Sitnica elementary school, yesterday you told the Court were you detained there for six or seven days. And that's at LiveNote page 81. Were you ever told during these six or seven days why you were being detained?

utterances.speaker: SAMIR DEDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. They didn't tell me personally. There was a lot of uncertainty, waiting. Nobody said anything. And then on that last day that we were there, they just told us that we were going to be exchanged for some Serb soldiers, but this was just a trick in order to give us a little morale, but actually, the trip was completely different. We were being taken to the Manjaca camp.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How did you -- how were you taken to the Manjaca camp?

utterances.speaker: SAMIR DEDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was a very difficult trip. They brought us out of that school. They lined us up on the asphalt road and this took quite a while. There was mistreatment by the soldiers and also the villagers from that village, they all gathered there and they were throwing stones, and it was incredibly awful. Then they ordered us to go. It was a large group of people, over 350 persons. We were surrounded by their soldiers and policemen. We had to keep our hands always behind our backs and we set out on foot for Manjaca. That morning we didn't get anything to eat. We started out along forest roads and it was very strenuous. As we were walking through their villages, all the villagers would come out and insult us, curse us, call us balijas. It was the first time that I had heard that word. I didn't know what it meant. And they also threw stones. When we came through the woods, whoever was in front of us, we had to place our hands on the shoulders of the person in front of us so it was impossible to walk. People lost their shoes, their boots, whatever it was that they had on their feet. So that at the end of the trip, many people were without footwear and their feet were bloody from the stones. It was quite hot so that many people fainted during the trip. They ordered then that other people who were still on their feet, who were still walking, should carry these people who had fainted, and it was really terrible. Then we reached Dobrnja -- I think that's what the place was called, near Manjaca where their soldiers were stationed and that was the worst part to pass. They stopped the convoy, the soldiers, there were quite a few of them, and they simply wouldn't let us pass. They wanted to get their knives out to cut our throats, to kill. So the police officers who were escorting us started to fire into the air and only then did we manage to pass that point, pass those soldiers. And then at around 4.00, we reached the Manjaca concentration camp.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What time did you leave Sitnica?

utterances.speaker: SAMIR DEDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I wasn't -- I'm not exactly sure about the time but it was early, maybe it was 10.00, 10.30.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you take the route that one would have normally travelled from Sitnica to Manjaca?

utterances.speaker: SAMIR DEDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I took that road maybe once or twice on my way to Banja Luka. For a part of the trip we were walking on asphalt roads but the rest of the trip or most of the trip we took forest paths or roads and it was very strenuous and it was a road that I had never taken before.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was the distance between Sitnica and Manjaca, if you know? Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: SAMIR DEDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Later, in the stable where we were placed, we discussed this amongst ourselves. There were some older colleagues who worked before the war so it was -- they estimated that it was between 35 and 40 kilometres, but I'm not sure. This is what I heard.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Besides yourself, how many other underage persons were amongst you?

utterances.speaker: SAMIR DEDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I was released, another five or six people were released with me of my age, but according to my estimate, there were about 15 of us who were detained in the camp.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So there was approximately 15 young men with you on the trip. Do you know where they were from?

utterances.speaker: SAMIR DEDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know about two persons who were released with me. They were from a village.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter didn't get the name.

utterances.speaker: SAMIR DEDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: One of them was not 16 yet and the other one was the same age as me but we were not allowed to go around all the different stables and talk amongst ourselves.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm sorry, can you just repeat what village they were from?

utterances.speaker: SAMIR DEDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: About the two persons, I can say. They were from the village of Crljeni and they were released together with me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were there any elderly people on the trip between Sitnica and Manjaca?

utterances.speaker: SAMIR DEDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Are you talking about the others? They were also from the municipality of Kljuc.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Approximately how many elderly people were there in the convoy of 350?

utterances.speaker: SAMIR DEDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were a few, there were quite a few, quite a few people who were over 50 [Realtime transcript read in error "350"] and there were also from 15 to 20 people who were over 60, perhaps even more. There were people who were not able to walk. They couldn't walk for more than one kilometre.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I think you testified a moment ago that those people, the others had to carry; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SAMIR DEDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This is quite true. Some would carry these people for a stretch and then others would take over and carry them in order to help.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Ackerman?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Page 7, line 1, I'm sure he didn't say that there were people whose age were over 350.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Over 50.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Over 50, yes. Thank you, Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Dedic, you said there were quite a few people who were over 50 and there were also approximately 15 to 20 people who were over 60, perhaps even more; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SAMIR DEDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's true.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What happened when you arrived at the camp, Manjaca camp?

utterances.speaker: SAMIR DEDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When we got there, they took us into this walled in area, it was a large area. There were some stables there and they lined us up in front of them. Then there was a roll call and a head count. At that point, the sun was so strong that people started to faint, since we had been walking all day, we didn't have anything to eat. We didn't get any water. So that many people just fainted. Then they would just bring a bucket of water and throw it over that man who had fainted. And then after the names were taken down in that procedure, they ordered us to turn and face the stables and then they said who should go into which stable. This was accompanied by beatings and there were a lot of people on all sides. They brought us into those stables as if we were animals. You had to go in very quickly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When they took -- when you said that they took your names down, what other information did they obtain from you?

utterances.speaker: SAMIR DEDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: First name, last name, date of birth, and our -- the place where we came from, but they already had all that. They just had the list and then they went and covered the list.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you provide your father's name?

utterances.speaker: SAMIR DEDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. You had to give your father's name.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Which stable were you put into?

utterances.speaker: SAMIR DEDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was placed in the first line. There were three stables so I was in the second stable.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How many men were in that stable?

utterances.speaker: SAMIR DEDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were over 600 men.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I want to ask you some questions now about the conditions of the camp. How often were you provided food and what did it consist of?

utterances.speaker: SAMIR DEDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We didn't get anything the first day. They just shut us in. That first day was terrible. Night was falling so only the guards remained. Then they, at least in my stable and I think they did that in -- for each one, quite a lot of them came into the stable, they started to shout, to insult us, they told to us lie down on our stomachs with our head facing down, and to place our hands on our back. So these were stables where they kept livestock before, so it stank of manure even though it had been cleaned a couple of days before that so the smell was quite unpleasant. And then they went down along this concrete hall and whoever they wanted to take out, they would hit him on the head and they would tell him to get up and to leave. They took about five or ten people and started to mistreat them. Whoever from us others tried to raise their head to look, they would take that person out too. So we didn't dare to look at what they were doing. We could just hear the moans and screams of the people who were out there. This is how the first night passed. They stayed there perhaps for about an hour or so.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How long were you detained in Manjaca for? Approximately?

utterances.speaker: SAMIR DEDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Since we didn't have anything to tell time by or the date by, we didn't have watches, so it was difficult in all that fear to estimate the passage of time but I got home in the first half of July, perhaps by the 15th of July.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you went to Manjaca around the first week in June; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SAMIR DEDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So during this five or six week period, can you just describe to the Court what sort of food you were provided?

utterances.speaker: SAMIR DEDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can. Practically nothing. The following day, we received something, the meals consisted of breakfast, lunch, and dinner but it was quite minimal. We would get a plastic beaker with some tea, a little bit of tea on the bottom but it wasn't really tea. It was just warm water. It wasn't sweet or salty it just had a pale colour like it was weak tea and then we would get a small piece of bread. The bread was so hard that it was probably at least a week old or more. And then lunch was perhaps two or three spoonfuls of soup, sometimes beans. You get bread but the slice was so thin that you could see through it. Dinner was the same. If somebody tried to ask for more food, they would just be beaten more. The person would be so beaten that they had to be carried back to the stable. So that when people saw a couple of such cases, it didn't even cross their minds to ask for more food because they would only get a beating. This would be repeated the same day. There was no drinking water in the stables for five days. Running. When it was very hot, and the roofs of those stables had -- were of corrugated tin so it would get very, very hot and people would be thirsty and when we did get water it would be like rain water. It was cloudy and it almost smelled so that you couldn't really drink it. Because then later we would have stomach problems because of that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You mentioned yesterday that you weighed around 60 kilograms. What was your weight when you left the camp?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Kilograms?

utterances.speaker: SAMIR DEDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: During your detention, what were the hygiene conditions like? Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. Were you able to bathe?

utterances.speaker: SAMIR DEDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The hygiene wasn't up to much. I had a bath only once and that was outside. And this was maybe after about 20 days. There were ten people at the same time. There was one shower and ten people had to have a shower in two minutes so that many people didn't even manage to take their clothes off, and they had already then said that we needed to go back outside.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You mentioned that you had a bath only once and that was outside. Are you referring to the shower?

utterances.speaker: SAMIR DEDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, yes, yes, while I was there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were the detainees ever addressed as a group by anyone in authority?

utterances.speaker: SAMIR DEDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not by the authorities, but a person introduced himself as the camp commander. He didn't say his name. He just said that he was the camp commander. So he addressed us once when I was there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What did he say?

utterances.speaker: SAMIR DEDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the beginning, he pointed out to us that by coming to the camp, to the Manjaca camp, we had lost all our civil rights, our human rights, and that we would be treated like animals from that point on, that we didn't have the right to ask for anything or request anything, that we were only supposed to do what we were ordered to do. If anyone should request anything or ask for something, they would only be beaten. That's what he said.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you describe this man?

utterances.speaker: SAMIR DEDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember him vaguely. It was not a very tall person. He was a bit overweight. He had a mustache and he had a high voice. A high-pitched voice and he wore a camouflage uniform. This is what I remember. And I think that he was maybe a colonel by rank.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was the colour of his hair?

utterances.speaker: SAMIR DEDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Grey hair.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just one more question on hygiene. What toilet facilities were you provided with?

utterances.speaker: SAMIR DEDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was inside. There was a metal -- a tin barrel. The stable was divided into three parts. On the left and the right were people, and then in the middle there was a kind of cement floor, a concrete floor, so each of those sections had a barrel of its own so this is where we had to go, at least at night, because they wouldn't allow us to go outside at night.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you recall the names of any of the guards?

utterances.speaker: SAMIR DEDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember two of them, at least I understood that they were commanders of the guards, there was a person called Spaga and Fadil, Bula. These were maybe nicknames. I only remember the two of them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you give a physical description of Spaga?

utterances.speaker: SAMIR DEDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Medium height. He was not thin or fat. He was balding. He wore a black embroidered waist coat and probably that why they called him Spaga, Spaga meaning string.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How often were you addressed by the camp commander?

utterances.speaker: SAMIR DEDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: While I was there, twice, as far as I remember.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What happened during the night in your stable?

utterances.speaker: SAMIR DEDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I already said at the beginning, almost every night the guards would enter, take people out, and the scene was repeated every night, beatings, mistreatment.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you recall the names of anyone that was taken, called out from your stable?

utterances.speaker: SAMIR DEDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember two of them. Mirsad -- I can't remember his surname. He was a taxi driver in Kljuc. And Zaim, a vet, also in Kljuc. They were taken out most often and beaten up so that we remembered them well.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Could the witness be shown document marked P1110, please? It was disclosed under Witness 7.105.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Does your name appear on that document?

utterances.speaker: SAMIR DEDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it does, under number 54.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are any of these other names familiar to you, the other 54 names?

utterances.speaker: SAMIR DEDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do know them. I know Filipovic Omer, Leopold Flat, Bilic Alija, Filipovic Muhamed. And I may know quite a number of them by sight but I don't recognise the names.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you recall any of these family names being called out, either at the Nikolic -- Nikola Mackic school or at Sitnica school or at Manjaca?

utterances.speaker: SAMIR DEDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do remember. There were quite a number. For example, Kujundzic, Kumalic, Ticevic, Begic. Quite a number of family names. Egrlic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. I've finished with that document. Do you recall if any organisations visited the camp?

utterances.speaker: SAMIR DEDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This was shortly before I left. It was Merhamet from Banja Luka. I remember well. There were two men, I think. They came. They toured the stables. But they were advised not to talk to the detainees at all, just to pass through. So that it was just a formality. At one point, I heard the guards say to them, "Would you like to us keep you here for a while too, to see what it's like?" Even though this was a humanitarian or charitable organisation. They were there briefly and they left.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know whether Merhamet was aware that there were underage people being detained in Manjaca?

utterances.speaker: SAMIR DEDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know, because I couldn't communicate with them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did the ICRC, the International Red Cross, did they visit Manjaca camp while you were there?

utterances.speaker: SAMIR DEDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not while I was there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So what happened to you after your visit -- after the visit of Merhamet to the camp?

utterances.speaker: SAMIR DEDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: A day or two after their visit, a guard entered my stable. This was about mid-day, 11.00 or 12.00, and he called out my name and these other two young men, Esad Kablic and Fahrudin Omerovic and we got up and left the stable. He took us with him. We followed him. We reached the room where detainees were interrogated. It was a small room. We were each taken into different rooms then. This was a kind of formal interrogation by this interrogator, and as soon as I entered, he said to me, "Do you know you're going home?" I was surprised. And he said that when we got home, we should report and do our service in the Serbian army, and then a couple of other questions and then he said that we would be given some kind of certificates in Kljuc once we returned, and after this interrogation, we were taken back to the stable. We were not told when we would be going home. And the next day, in the afternoon, they again came to fetch us in the stable and they took us out. And they took us to a kind of minibus, a small bus, which came from Kljuc and it had the inscription elementary school Velegic. They took us inside. There were two policemen and the driver. He was also wearing a camouflage uniform. We were not told anything, what was happening, where we were going, so that it was absolutely vague. Again, we had to keep our heads down with our hands behind our head, and then they set off with us. After a certain period of time, we stopped at a checkpoint, a checkpoint held by their army, and it was being manned with people wearing olive-grey uniforms and I noticed through the window they were showing with their hands to the driver that he should bring us out for them to slaughter us, so that we were terribly frightened. We only just survived that trip, never mind that he showed them some sort of a certificate. They held us there for a while. And then we started up again. There were another couple of checkpoints, which we passed through more easily than this one, and then we arrived in Kljuc. It was already dusk. They drove us to the police station in Kljuc and we were told to wait in the bus. We were there alone. However, the town seemed deserted.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you -- I'm sorry, were you provided at the police station with this certificate?

utterances.speaker: SAMIR DEDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. After sometime, we waited in the bus. People were banging on the windows, that is soldiers, they were threatening to kill us, to slit our throats. We were alone in the bus. Then after sometime, this policeman came, carrying some papers, and he handed out those papers to Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. us. Then the three of us were driven to the bridge at Kljuc on the exit from the town. There is an intersection. One road leading to my village from that bridge it's about 11 kilometres to my village and he simply said that from there on we should go on foot. We didn't know at all what the situation was like in the town, and in the environs because we had been at Manjaca. It was only later that I realised why they released us in the nighttime and let us go on foot alone. We had our heads shaved already at Manjaca. They put some powder on our heads, allegedly for hygienic purposes and then they released us there and we set off on foot towards our village.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just going back to the police station and the certificate that you received, what did it state on the certificate?

utterances.speaker: SAMIR DEDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is only once I got home that I read it. It was compiled in such a way as to conceal those crimes, the fact that they had detained minors and elderly people and it just said that on that day, when we were released from Manjaca, that we had been taken into custody in our own homes and interrogated in the police station in Kljuc and released the same day. So the entire period we had spent at Manjaca is not mentioned anywhere. It was concealed. So that certificate didn't mean anything. You couldn't prove that you had spent any time there because there was no mention of Manjaca. Simply this taking into custody and release on the same day.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what happened to that certificate?

utterances.speaker: SAMIR DEDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I lost it at home, due to the fear and everything else. I couldn't find it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who else was released with you on that day? You mentioned the three underage persons. Was there anyone else that was released with you?

utterances.speaker: SAMIR DEDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were the three of us from my village, myself and another two, and another two or three minors. Five or six minors and as many elderly people, so a total of some ten men were released. I only remember the names of these two because they are from my village.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Can the witness be shown a document which has been marked P1111? I'm sorry, excuse me. I'm sorry, Exhibit P330.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Prior to yesterday, had you ever seen that document before?

utterances.speaker: SAMIR DEDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What is the date of the document and the title of the document?

utterances.speaker: SAMIR DEDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The date is the 1st of October, 1992, and it coincides with my date of birth. I never saw this before. The request for the abolition of Muslim detainees put up in Manjaca. I don't know what kind of rebellion they mentioned, against which republic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you just read the first paragraph, please?

utterances.speaker: SAMIR DEDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "The Republika Srpska assembly of the Autonomous Region of Krajina, Banja Luka."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm sorry, after, to the Presidency of Republika Srpska, request for pardon for Muslim prisoners kept at Manjaca. Can you read the paragraph below that?

utterances.speaker: SAMIR DEDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. "We are requesting that you pardon and release the following detainees kept in Manjaca, because it has been established that they did not take part in the revolt against Republika Srpska."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Does your name appear on that document?

utterances.speaker: SAMIR DEDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It does, under number 12.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you aware of anyone else detained in Manjaca that had the same name as you?

utterances.speaker: SAMIR DEDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I was not.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who is the document signed by, if you are able to read the typing?

utterances.speaker: SAMIR DEDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's rather black, Vojo Kupresanin.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: If the witness could now be shown the document marked P1111?

utterances.speaker: SAMIR DEDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: May I say something else in connection with this document?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: SAMIR DEDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The date, the 1st of October, on top, and on the bottom, on the 9th of October, by then I was already in the Republic of Slovenia, staying with relatives. And from there, I went to Germany to stay with my father.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If you could now look at P1111, what is the date of that document?

utterances.speaker: SAMIR DEDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: 7th of October, 1992.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And this is a list of released and pardoned persons. Does your name appear on that document?

utterances.speaker: SAMIR DEDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It does, under number 7.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you read the paragraph below the names, please?

utterances.speaker: SAMIR DEDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Do I have to? "Pursuant to the decision of the Presidency of Republika Srpska, number 01-1074/92, of 2nd October" -- this is probably 1992, but it's black -- "on abolition, the above named persons were released from prison and according to the same decision, they should be allowed to leave the territory of Republika Srpska through the International Committee of the Red Cross in Banja Luka."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And again, who is that document signed by?

utterances.speaker: SAMIR DEDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The same person, Vojo Kupresanin.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. I've finished with that document. I now want to ask you some questions about when you were released from Manjaca camp.

utterances.speaker: SAMIR DEDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Just a moment, please. The International Red Cross never took me anywhere. As it says here.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. I now want to ask you some questions about when you returned to your village after you were released from Manjaca. You said that were you dropped at the crossroads and made your way back to the village. What was the condition of your house when you returned in mid-July?

utterances.speaker: SAMIR DEDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: May I go back a little to this intersection of the road? Because I haven't finished that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Please.

utterances.speaker: SAMIR DEDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: From that crossroads, we headed home, not knowing what the situation was like. Of course, looking forward to our going home, but the situation was quite the opposite. That night, when we left, we probably would not have arrived home alive. It was our good fortune that a man, a Muslim, there was a village called Zgon, a hamlet called Mehmedagici, right next to the crossroads and a man waved to us and told us to come to him. Though I may not have mentioned this in my statement but later on, I remembered. And then he took us to his own house and first he asked us who we were, where we were coming from, and he assumed that we had been in some sort of detention because we had our heads shaved. And then he asked us where we were heading and we said that we were from the village of Crljeni and that we were going home, and he said at this time of night, it's not advisable to go there, because from the Separacija which was a company manufacturing concrete and along the road, there were their trenches and their soldiers, and if you go, they will shoot at you as soon as you approach, and this was all planned for them to release us in the nighttime and let us go and then we would get killed and nobody would know what had happened to us. So he saved us from that and we spent the night there. And the next morning, about 9.00, he told us to go ahead, so that at Suknjiste, a couple of houses along the Sana River, as they are called, we already came across the first checkpoint. And they stopped us there. They asked us a few questions, we showed them these certificates, and they let us go on. We even came across two or three of their soldiers sleeping next to the trenches. So it was rather ridiculous, but we didn't dare do anything. I don't know what kind of an army they were. So we just simply went along our way.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And at some point, you reached your house; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SAMIR DEDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was the condition of your house?

utterances.speaker: SAMIR DEDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was like all the other houses, riddled with bullet holes. The roof was damaged. Most of the windows broken. And I heard later from my mother that they had shelled the village from the other side of Plamenica, Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. and the villages where they had fired shells and opened fire. I saw that many things were missing from the house. They had been taken. Many houses were damaged, almost all of them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Had your house been looted?

utterances.speaker: SAMIR DEDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Mostly, yes, I said mostly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Your mother, your younger brother and sister were there. Did you stay in the house with them?

utterances.speaker: SAMIR DEDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That first day, I stayed with them. Already in the evening, when it became dark, at least that was the situation in the village, and the other villagers said it was dangerous for men to spend the night at home. So that we, together with the others, there were another ten or so elderly men and the three of us, so we spent the night outside of the village, though maybe this was even more dangerous, but we felt safer because if they came and they would come to the village often during the day and the night, they would search the house and if they found anyone, there was a high probability of them being taken away in an unknown direction.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you say they would come to the village often during the day and night, who are you referring to?

utterances.speaker: SAMIR DEDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Serbs, the Serb soldiers. There was no one else in the village. The men were in detention. Everyone, the birds knew that they were Serbs. Who would be shooting.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How would they come?

utterances.speaker: SAMIR DEDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In vehicles.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What sort of vehicles?

utterances.speaker: SAMIR DEDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember most, a red bus, and when it arrived, we knew it would take someone from the village and we all hid when we saw the bus arriving.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was this a big bus?

utterances.speaker: SAMIR DEDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it was a small, a minibus.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were any of the religious buildings in Kljuc damaged or destroyed between May and September, 1992, that you are aware of?

utterances.speaker: SAMIR DEDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The mosque was completely destroyed to the foundations, the mosque in my village was also quite damaged.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know -- do you recall when the mosque in Kljuc was damaged, in Kljuc town?

utterances.speaker: SAMIR DEDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It was in August, I don't remember the date.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know how it was damaged?

utterances.speaker: SAMIR DEDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This happened during the night. I was close to the village, in a little wood, maybe about 100 metres away from my house. The house of my two uncles was there as well, not too far away. At one point I decided to go to my uncle's house because it was empty. He was in Slovenia with his family. I wanted to drink some water. While entering the house, the window faced the town of Kljuc, and it was -- there was moonlight so it was possible to see the old town quite well. At one point, the house shook as by an earthquake. The glass shook and some of the glass shattered. At that moment, I saw a big flash from the valley where the town of Kljuc is. It was a flash, a very big flash. I immediately assumed that it was some big building. Later, I heard from my mother, who was in Kljuc that night, she was spending the night at a relative's, so near the mosque where she was, this house was about 500 metres away from the mosque so when she came back to our house, she said that that night the mosque had been knocked down, that it was a very powerful blast, that she was quite close and the next day on her way back home she saw the surrounding buildings, they were apartment buildings around the mosque, made of brick, so she could see a lot of rubble and shattered glass around those buildings. Perhaps the rubble had been thrown about 150 metres away. The mosque was completely destroyed together with the minaret.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was the name of this mosque, if you know?

utterances.speaker: SAMIR DEDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know the name. The Kljuc mosque, something like that. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where was it situated? What street? Do you know?

utterances.speaker: SAMIR DEDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember the street. It was on the way to Haribacic [phoen] which is a settlement in Kljuc. And maybe about 200 metres to the left of the mosque is the medical centre. It's still there today, the Kljuc medical centre.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When did you leave the Kljuc municipality?

utterances.speaker: SAMIR DEDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was in early September or perhaps mid-September. It was September in any case.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And how did you leave?

utterances.speaker: SAMIR DEDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In a convoy.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who organised this convoy?

utterances.speaker: SAMIR DEDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. They probably organised it, the Serbs. There was nobody else to help those people. It wasn't possible to live there any longer. And they wanted to cleanse that area of Muslims and Croats. And that's probably why they did it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How did you get on to the convoy? What steps did you have to take in order to leave?

utterances.speaker: SAMIR DEDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was a fairly difficult process. My mother went to Kljuc. I think she went to the municipal office. There was a long line in front of the municipal building and according to what she said, they were mistreated, cursed at. She had to sign a document that she was voluntarily giving up the house and everything that we owned, voluntarily, although she didn't really feel that way, but this is what she had to do in order to get a ticket for the convoy. So if you didn't sign, you couldn't leave. So you had to give up everything that you owned.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How many people left Kljuc when you did? The day you left. Approximately how many people were on that convoy?

utterances.speaker: SAMIR DEDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were a lot of people. There were about seven buses and three or four large trailer trucks, carrying men, women, children, the elderly, packed together like sardines. We were practically one on top of the other. It was impossible. It was as if they were loading potatoes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where did the buses and trucks end up? Where did the convoy go?

utterances.speaker: SAMIR DEDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the end of the journey, which took all day, when it was almost night, we got to a pretty high plateau. I'm not sure where that was. We weren't able to see where we were. I was in the truck under the tarpaulin so I wasn't able to see anything. We were hit with stones. Any place that we passed through, we were hit by stones. So a lot of people in the convoy were injured. The tarpaulin is pretty thin so people did get hit. So when we got to that plateau, we were let out from the buses and the trucks, and brought to a large precipice, a high precipice, and from the top you could see the canyon. And they told us to proceed slowly. There were many people there, men, women, children, the elderly and the road itself was rocky and it was very difficult to walk along it, particularly for the elderly, the path was very narrow so that many women and children and the elderly slipped and fell so we had to help them. Because each person had one or two bags, what they managed to take with them. So it was very difficult to walk down the canyon. At one point, when we -- when I reached the precipice I heard one of the soldiers say to another soldier, "Look at how many young people we are releasing. And we could have killed them all here and thrown them down from these rocks and nobody would know." I was just waiting for the moment when somebody would fire in my back but thank God this didn't happen.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know the name of the plateau?

utterances.speaker: SAMIR DEDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Later, when I reached Travnik, I found out that this was a plateau of Mount Vlasic close to the town of Skender Vakuf. That was the last stop. This is what I found out when I got there, so --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm sorry?

utterances.speaker: SAMIR DEDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: So this town of Travnik, where we ended up was in a valley at the bottom of the canyon. That was our last -- our destination.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was anyone injured or killed on your convoy?

utterances.speaker: SAMIR DEDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've already mentioned injuries that they threw stones, quite large stones, at the tarpaulin so that a lot of people were struck in the face. A person had two or three teeth knocked out right away, lips were cut. Before we reached the plateau at one point, the convoy was stopped. They opened each trailer-truck and they lifted up the tarpaulin. They Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. were looking for one person. And I remember his last flame was Potic [as interpreted] and they asked whether he was in our truck. He wasn't in our truck. So they went along further asking about him. And then later, only two shots were heard, maybe one or two shots were heard, after two or three minutes or maybe five minutes after they had started to look for this man. I found out from his family in Travnik that that man never reached Travnik and he was in this convoy.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You mentioned the name Potic is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SAMIR DEDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. No, no. The correct name is Hotic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: After you arrived in Travnik, did any other convoys from Kljuc municipality arrive in Travnik?

utterances.speaker: SAMIR DEDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Convoys went before ours and after ours, until they cleansed everything. I don't know how many people remained behind but very few of them did remain behind. People who couldn't leave because they were too old or they simply couldn't afford to buy this ticket which cost 50 marks or something like that, so they were unable to leave. The entire town was -- people left from that whole town.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: My final question to you: Was there any armed resistance in your village that you are aware of?

utterances.speaker: SAMIR DEDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember. I don't know anything about that. I went to school, like I said a few times before. I didn't have any weapons. I only saw those seven soldiers being taken through the village because my house is close it to the road. They were not mistreated. I saw that with my own eyes. They were treated properly and I found out about that and they were handed over to the UNPROFOR in the -- in the village of --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter didn't hear the village.

utterances.speaker: SAMIR DEDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: But they were treated correctly. Some of those people who were captured, they are good people everywhere, so in the camp, they would give a packet of cigarettes to some people from our village where they had been detained because they were treated nicely by those people. This is what I heard from people from the village who had this happen to them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just going back to when you said that the soldiers had been captured and were handed over to UNPROFOR. The interpreter missed the village. Which village did you say?

utterances.speaker: SAMIR DEDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think they were handed over to UNPROFOR in the village of Krasulje. This is what I heard. And then they processed them after that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And so during your whole detention, you were never, ever informed as to why you were being detained?

utterances.speaker: SAMIR DEDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I would like to go back a little bit. When the commander spoke to us, it was very humiliating. He said that our bones would be left up there, that we would be killed, that we were dirtying the Serb land. That's what he said. Because we were Muslims.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Sutherland. We have two options. Either Mr. Trbojevic starts the cross-examination right away and then we break after ten minutes or we break now and he starts the cross-examination soon after the break. It's your choice.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRBOJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm in your hands.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So you make it my choice?

utterances.speaker: MR. TRBOJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. We break now. We give the interpreters a break because it has been quite a difficult morning for them. I could notice from behind the glass here. We will resume -- you will start your cross-examination immediately after the break. May I suggest to you, with your indulgence that we have a shorter break than usual, 20 minutes instead of 30? All right? Okay. So it's 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So Mr. Dedic, as I tried to explain to you yesterday, now it's the turn of the Defence attorney for Radoslav Brdjanin to cross-examine you. Mr. Trbojevic, I understand, will be cross-examining you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRBOJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So please, Mr. Trbojevic, go ahead. Cross-examined by Mr. Trbojevic:

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Do you want to hand it over?

utterances.speaker: MR. TRBOJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, it won't be necessary.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRBOJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I would like to go back to the beginning of these events, to the 26th and the 27th of May. You told us that you saw captured Serb soldiers?

utterances.speaker: SAMIR DEDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But you didn't tell us who captured them?

utterances.speaker: SAMIR DEDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Since I wasn't there, I'm not able to say who it was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In the statement that you provided to the Prosecution on the 4th of June, 2001, you say that you saw them passing from a distance of about 50 metres?

utterances.speaker: SAMIR DEDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is true.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the speakers please slow down.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, every time I have to take care of this. Mr. Trbojevic and Mr. Dedic, you both speak the same language. And you're not giving each other time enough -- enough time between answer and question. You're just firing an answer which is immediately followed by question and then answer and then question. You're not being nice to the interpreters. The interpreters have to translate into English and into French. So when Mr. Trbojevic puts a question to you, Mr. Dedic, please allow some time before you answer, just a short interval of time, to give the interpreters time, a chance to translate to us. And the same applies to you, Mr. Trbojevic, and this is not the first time I'm pointing this out. When the witness has finished his reply, his answer, please allow an interval. Otherwise we will have to do it otherwise and I wouldn't like to intervene unless it is absolutely necessary. So Mr. Trbojevic, question.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRBOJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The last question was who was taking these -- who was in charge of these soldiers?

utterances.speaker: SAMIR DEDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The people from the village were.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were these people armed?

utterances.speaker: SAMIR DEDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't see that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm asking you is it possible that a group of soldiers is being escorted by another group of people and that you don't know whether this other group of people was armed or not? Is that possible?

utterances.speaker: SAMIR DEDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said I didn't see it, so if I didn't see it, I didn't see it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said that after these soldiers were captured, there was fear in the village and this was the reason why the whole village moved across the river. Is this true?

utterances.speaker: SAMIR DEDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you explain to us why there was this fear?

utterances.speaker: SAMIR DEDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was fear simply because these soldiers had been captured. They had an objective. This is what I heard later, an attack on the village, so it's normal for panic to come about.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you afraid of reprisal?

utterances.speaker: SAMIR DEDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I personally wasn't, because I didn't take part in this. This was an attack on the village, against the population, which was just carrying out its every day duties.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were these soldiers captured during an attack on the village?

utterances.speaker: SAMIR DEDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't say because I didn't take part in that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But you were in the village.

utterances.speaker: SAMIR DEDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was in the village, in my house, maybe about one kilometre away from the place where they were captured.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was there any shooting that you heard?

utterances.speaker: SAMIR DEDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I could hear it but I couldn't determine from which Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. direction it was coming from. There was shooting every day. There was shooting from Serb villages.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You're being good for precisely two minutes and a half. And now you're falling back to what I tried to convince you to avoid. Please, Mr. Trbojevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRBOJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I wanted to ask whether anybody was wounded during this capture.

utterances.speaker: SAMIR DEDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I could see, no, no one was injured.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you maybe hear about it later?

utterances.speaker: SAMIR DEDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I didn't hear later that anybody had been wounded.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Later, you told us that through the window of the house, you saw several different uniforms. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: SAMIR DEDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This was in the village of Plamenica.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. You said camouflage uniforms, olive-grey uniforms, police uniforms. So I'm asking you whether the police uniforms that you saw were the regular blue uniforms as well as the camouflage uniforms.

utterances.speaker: SAMIR DEDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't know. I'm not a military analyst. I know that there were blue uniforms, blue police uniforms, then camouflage uniforms. I don't know whether they were army or police camouflage uniforms. And a lot of uniforms belonging to the police reserves, blue uniforms, but they were different from the regular blue police uniforms.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You also mentioned red berets?

utterances.speaker: SAMIR DEDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. In the town of Kljuc.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what were the men with the red berets -- what kind of uniforms were they wearing?

utterances.speaker: SAMIR DEDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Camouflage uniforms also.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Green or blue?

utterances.speaker: SAMIR DEDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would say they were blue, although this was a long time ago but I think that they were blue.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said that you heard that this was supposed to be some kind of special police force from Banja Luka?

utterances.speaker: SAMIR DEDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you explain to us how you found this out?

utterances.speaker: SAMIR DEDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: While talking to some people in the town on my way to school, to the station, we saw them constantly, so at one point we asked who they were, why were they firing in the town, why were they frightening the people. So we simply concluded that they appeared around the town suddenly, they had to have -- had to have come from somewhere so that's what we heard.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you able to see military units going towards Kupres or towards Croatia?

utterances.speaker: SAMIR DEDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On one occasion, on my way from school to the bus station, I saw a large convoy of buses and trucks going through town.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you know which units these were?

utterances.speaker: SAMIR DEDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. We knew. Mostly it was the Serb army reserve units. We were familiar with the uniforms, olive-grey uniforms, and they also fired into the air from the bus windows. They raised three fingers in the air so it could be clearly seen whose units they were.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you have the opportunity of seeing these units when they were coming back from Kupres and Croatia?

utterances.speaker: SAMIR DEDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes. We could all feel that, since we knew when they would be coming to Kljuc, they rioted throughout the town. They fired. Most of them were drunk. They simply installed a reign of terror.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were these local reserve forces or were there recruits from other parts of the former Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: SAMIR DEDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were quite a number that I knew and others that I didn't know, of course. There were a lot of men.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: One of the witnesses told us where those seven captured prisoners were from, soldiers were from. Had you heard perhaps where they were from?

utterances.speaker: SAMIR DEDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't hear exactly where they were from but according to what people said, much later, I heard that they were from the region between Sitnica and Banja Luka. That area. That is at least what I heard. And that -- I seem to remember that there was one from Montenegro but who lived in Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you tell me, please, when they interrogated you at the Mackic elementary school, who interrogated you?

utterances.speaker: SAMIR DEDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I just know that the man was wearing a uniform. I don't know his name and I didn't know him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What kind of uniform?

utterances.speaker: SAMIR DEDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Camouflage uniform.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Green or blue?

utterances.speaker: SAMIR DEDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In a green uniform was the one who questioned me but I saw quite a number wearing blue and all kinds of uniforms.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You mentioned insignia on those uniforms. Were they insignia that you saw at the time or were they insignia that you noticed later?

utterances.speaker: SAMIR DEDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: One could notice them at the time. Mostly on the shoulder, there was the Serbian flag, and the four Cyrillic S's.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you describe in what greater detail this flag on the soldier?

utterances.speaker: SAMIR DEDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: A small badge, like an emblem, stuck on to the shirt or whatever.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And those four S's?

utterances.speaker: SAMIR DEDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The flag, on the flag there was a cross and the 4 S's in the four corners.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The Prosecutor asked you yesterday about Mr. Omer Filipovic in Sitnica.

utterances.speaker: SAMIR DEDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In your statement to the OTP, you described how you saw him. It seems to me that yesterday you didn't quite repeat that in the same way.

utterances.speaker: SAMIR DEDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because she didn't ask me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. I'm asking you. How did you see him?

utterances.speaker: SAMIR DEDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was rather beaten up and he was covered in blood. That is how I saw him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are you sure of that?

utterances.speaker: SAMIR DEDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am sure.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If I tell you that his brother claimed that in Stara Gradiska when they met, he told him that he hadn't been beaten, do you still say that you saw him in Sitnica bloodied?

utterances.speaker: SAMIR DEDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do. I saw the man who was black and blue in the face.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, I object to Mr. Trbojevic putting what other witnesses say to the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I wouldn't sustain your -- because first the witness -- I wouldn't sustain your objection, because it's perfectly legitimate. He is trying to confront the witness with the statement that he has just made now, that he stands by his written statement to the Prosecution that he saw Omer Filipovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think he can still make the same point in cross-examination without referring to other witnesses who have testified previously.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: He's perfectly entitled to do that. Provided he does not mislead something that has already been in the record of the case and provided he's not misleading the witness he's perfectly entitled to do it. Yes, Mr. Trbojevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRBOJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's in the record. And I just told the witness this. And asked him whether he stood by what he said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Do you want to say anything, Mr. Ackerman?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I probably shouldn't but I should say the only care that needs to be exercised is the names of protected witnesses are not mentioned but this was not a protect witness, so that's -- I think that's what Ms. Sutherland is concerned about.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That's your concern. I don't think that's her concern. It's a procedural matter that the witness should not be told what other witnesses have stated. But I see nothing wrong with that. It's accepted in several jurisdictions and in several systems and I would allow it. Yes, Mr. Trbojevic. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRBOJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation].

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In your statement to the OTP, you mention the bad conditions at Manjaca. Among other things, you said that there was typhoid fever an yellow fever widespread among the detainees there?

utterances.speaker: SAMIR DEDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you a witness of that, an eyewitness of that?

utterances.speaker: SAMIR DEDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: While I was there, there were already cases among the men who had yellow fever. They were sent to Banja Luka to hospital, something like that. While I was there, and typhoid fever developed later. I heard that when after I left, talking to colleagues, I heard about that, but I was an eyewitness of yellow fever.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRBOJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the witness be shown Exhibit P1110, please?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It's the list of detainees from Kljuc. You told us that among the detainees, there were about some 15 minors, people underage; is that right?

utterances.speaker: SAMIR DEDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you please look at the date of birth of the people there and see how many you can find who were underage? I was not able to find anyone else except you.

utterances.speaker: SAMIR DEDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. But this is a list of 54 men, and from the Kljuc municipality, as far as I know, there were 1.300 detainees.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We don't need it any more. Thank you. You spoke of the need to sign a statement renouncing all rights to property as a precondition for leaving Kljuc.

utterances.speaker: SAMIR DEDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is there any such statement to be found? Do you have one?

utterances.speaker: SAMIR DEDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't have one because at the time all that was important was to save one's life. As for documents which didn't really mean anything, they only meant something for the authorities in Kljuc who required them. Nobody cared about them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know exactly what that statement said?

utterances.speaker: SAMIR DEDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do know exactly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you tell us, please?

utterances.speaker: SAMIR DEDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I saw the statement which my mother brought for our family, and it stated that she has to renounce all property that she owned and the land as well, voluntarily. Otherwise, we would not be allowed to buy these tickets and to leave Kljuc.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All of that was in that statement?

utterances.speaker: SAMIR DEDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, all this was stated in that statement, as it probably also our names, my mother's, my own, my brother's and my sister's, because all four of us were on this list.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If I tell you that there are certain regulations as to how property rights can be transferred and that they cannot be done in that way, would you agree with me that that statement had no legal validity?

utterances.speaker: SAMIR DEDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The authorities in Kljuc who required this and who forced us to do that, to save our lives --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said that the Serbs wanted to cleanse the area of Muslims and Croats.

utterances.speaker: SAMIR DEDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's what they in fact did, too.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The demand to leave the dangerous area, as you said, in a convoy, were they designed to save your lives or to cleanse the area?

utterances.speaker: SAMIR DEDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as we were concerned, we wanted to save our lives. I don't know what they meant, because we didn't know where we were going.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You told us that some persons stoned the convoy as you went by.

utterances.speaker: SAMIR DEDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That is quite true.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Trucks that were covered with tarpaulin?

utterances.speaker: SAMIR DEDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you able to see who those people were?

utterances.speaker: SAMIR DEDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't see who they were.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could we please go back to another event very briefly? You told us that your village was about 13 kilometres from Kljuc. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: SAMIR DEDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said that you went to your uncle's house to take some water when there was an explosion in Kljuc; is that right?

utterances.speaker: SAMIR DEDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And that the windows shook and some broke as a result of that explosion, on that house. That's what you said.

utterances.speaker: SAMIR DEDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is what I said.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If I tell you that at a distance of 13 kilometres it is impossible for the windows to shake because in that case, nothing would be left of Kljuc, do you still stand by what you said?

utterances.speaker: SAMIR DEDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRBOJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have no further questions, Your Honours. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Trbojevic. Is there re-examination?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So that brings us to the end of your testimony here as I expected and told you yesterday it would be. On behalf of the -- this Tribunal, I would like to thank you for having accepted to come here and give evidence. You will now be attended to, escorted out of the courtroom and given all the necessary attention you require in order to be able to return to your country. I thank you once more.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you too.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Is the next witness already in line, Madam Richterova?

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: I hope so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Do you think we will finish with him today?

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: I also hope that we will finish.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I now am asking you a very simple question because the one after this, the next one is still open, the one after is not, if I remember well.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Yes, you're right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think we would need to advise a little bit the technicians. Any way, if they need to attend to that today or whether they need not bother about it today. All right? It's being taken care of? Okay. I thank you. So let's bring in the next witness. The usher, I suppose, will do that. Yes, Mr. Ackerman?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: While we are waiting may I just take care after little business?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I'm not sure it's been filed yet but there is a document in the Appeals Chamber -- maybe you're not even the person, I think you are though. There is a document filed in the Appeals Chamber requesting that the portions of the transcripts of this week, which deal with the Randal matter be released to counsel for Randal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And that's because most of it was in private session, I suppose.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Yes, and I have no objection to that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. I thank you, Mr. Ackerman. I suppose there is no objection forthcoming from the Prosecution either?

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. But this, I don't like. I am not used to receiving communications directly from the lawyers to the Honourable Judges. There should be a document -- this is not -- this is created by the office? But this is a letter which is sent directly from the law firm to the Honourable Justices, whoever they may be, and I do not frankly know whether it's just the three of us and if - you can bring in the witness, please - whether it's just the three of us here in this trial or whether it's the Honourable Justices in the Appeals Chamber and in any case, there should be a proper motion and not a letter directed -- addressed straight to the Judges. But they file a motion. I mean, because this is a direct communication with the Justices and I don't like it. You don't write a letter and say, "Please consider this correspondence as a motion or request by Jonathan Randal for a release of the transcript to this firm and counsel for Mr. Randal only." They file a proper motion. So we will not entertain it, for sure. We will take -- we have taken notice of the non-objection from either side but --

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, at the moment the Prosecution doesn't have a copy of the correspondence.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: It's being filed at the moment so I can give you one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It needs to be a proper motion filed in the proper Chamber with an ad hoc request addressed to who is in a position to accede or reject that request.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm sorry, the Prosecution can contact the instructing solicitors and ask them to file the requisite motion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. I thank you for cooperating, Ms. Sutherland.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So good morning to you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And welcome to this Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You know the reason for your presence here. You're going to give evidence.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And it is my duty as the Presiding Judge to tell you before you start giving evidence that our rules require that you first enter -- make a solemn declaration to speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth during your testimony. The text of this solemn declaration which for all intents and purposes is the equivalent of an oath is contained in a piece of paper which the usher is going to hand to you now. And could you please be kind enough to read that solemn declaration? And that will be your undertaking to this Tribunal to tell us the truth and the whole truth.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you. You may sit down. Very simply I'll try to explain what's going to happen. We are the three judges dealing with this case and we will ultimately be the ones to decide this case. The case has been instituted by the Prosecutor against Radoslav Brdjanin, and you will be examined first by means of a series of questions by the Prosecution. The officer -- senior officer from the Prosecution who will be conducting the examination-in-chief, what we call the examination-in-chief, is the lady who is sitting in the middle at your right, Madam Richterova, who I suppose you've met already. When the examination-in-chief is over, then, as of right, the Defence for the accused, the lawyers for the accused, have a right to cross examine you. In other words to put questions to you as well. You have no right to distinguish between questions forthcoming from the Prosecution or questions coming from the Defence. Your duty is to answer each and every question as truthfully as possible. And as accurately as possible. Unless we tell you not to answer the question. We are here to hear your story. We are also here to protect you if need be. So we will stop anyone putting to you any questions that could potentially harass you but I can assure you that that has not happened so far in the ten months that this case has been going on. So you don't need to worry. Just sit down, relax, and we can start with the examination-in-chief. Madam Richterova, the witness is in your hands.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour, but before I start I would like to ask you when you plan the next break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We started at ten past 11.00. So we will break at, I suppose, half 12.00 or -- yeah. Any way, let's go on and we'll see.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: I just wanted to know approximately how to plan.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
